title: David Livingstone Across Africa
intro: David Livingstone, a Scottish doctor and missionary with the London Missionary Society, travelled north from Linyanti with Kololo men lent by their chief Sekeletu to look for a trade route to the coast. He crossed south-central Africa from the Atlantic to the Indian Ocean, then returned for a Zambezi expedition and a last search for the sources of the Nile.
ending: Livingstone died on 1 May 1873 in Chief Chitambo's village at Chipundu. His attendants Chuma and Susi buried his heart there and carried his body and papers to Bagamoyo on the coast, from where it went by ship to Britain.

legs.title: From Linyanti to the Atlantic and the Indian Ocean

stops.text: The party reached the Portuguese city of Luanda on the Atlantic after great difficulties, and Livingstone nearly died of fever on the way. He judged the route too hard for future traders.
stops.quote: They reached the Portuguese city of Luanda on the Atlantic in May 1854 after profound difficulties and the near-death of Livingstone from fever.

stops.text: Going east down the Zambezi, Livingstone became the first European to see the waterfall called Mosi-oa-Tunya, "the smoke that thunders". He named it Victoria Falls after Queen Victoria.
stops.quote: Mosi-oa-Tunya ("the smoke that thunders") waterfall, which he named Victoria Falls after Queen Victoria.

stops.text: Livingstone reached Quelimane on the Indian Ocean, having mapped most of the course of the Zambezi. He was hailed as the first European to cross south-central Africa at that latitude.
stops.quote: He successfully reached Quelimane on the Indian Ocean, having mapped most of the course of the Zambezi river.

stops.text: The expedition left Britain on the steamer Pearl with the prefabricated river steamer Ma Robert. At Freetown they took on 12 Kru seafarers to man the river steamer.
stops.quote: They left on 10 March, at Freetown collected 12 Kru seafarers to man the river steamer, and reached the Zambezi on 14 May.

stops.text: The Zambezi proved impassable to boats past the Cahora Bassa rapids. The experts were stuck at Shupanga and quarrelled, and the artist Thomas Baines was dismissed from the expedition.
stops.quote: The experts, stuck at Shupanga, could not make the intended progress, and there were disagreements. Artist Thomas Baines was dismissed from the expedition.

stops.text: Livingstone returned to Africa at Zanzibar, where the Sultan provided a house for his use while he prepared an expedition to seek the source of the Nile.
stops.quote: Livingstone House in Stone Town, Zanzibar, provided by the Sultan for Livingstone's use, January to March 1866, to prepare his last expedition

stops.text: His assistants had gradually deserted him. He reached Lake Malawi after most of his supplies, including all his medicines, had been stolen.
stops.quote: He reached Lake Malawi on 6 August, by which time most of his supplies had been stolen, including all his medicines.

stops.text: Livingstone, forced by ill health to travel with slave traders, arrived at Lake Mweru. He went on south to become the first European to see Lake Bangweulu.
stops.quote: He arrived at Lake Mweru on 8 November 1867 and continued on, travelling south to become the first European to see Lake Bangweulu.

stops.text: At the Nyangwe market on the Lualaba River, Livingstone watched Arab slavers massacre around 400 Africans, standing beside the trader Dugumbe. The killing horrified him and left him too shattered to continue his search.
stops.quote: On 15 July 1871, Livingstone recorded in his field diary his immediate impressions as he witnessed around 400 Africans being massacred by Arab slavers at the Nyangwe market on the banks of the Lualaba River

stops.text: Livingstone travelled 240 miles (390 km) back from Nyangwe to Ujiji, an Arab settlement on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika, violently ill most of the way.
stops.quote: he travelled 240 miles (390 km) from Nyangwe back to Ujiji, an Arab settlement on the eastern shore of Lake Tanganyika—violently ill most of the way—arriving on 23 October 1871.

stops.text: Henry Morton Stanley, sent by the New York Herald, found Livingstone at Ujiji. Despite Stanley's urgings, Livingstone would not leave Africa until his mission was complete.
stops.quote: He found Livingstone in Ujiji on 10 November 1871

stops.text: Livingstone died in Chief Chitambo's village from malaria and internal bleeding due to dysentery. Chuma and Susi removed his heart and buried it under a tree near where he died.
stops.quote: Livingstone died on 1 May 1873 at age 60 in Chief Chitambo's village at Chipundu, southeast of Lake Bangweulu, in present-day Zambia

stops.text: Chuma and Susi's expedition carried his remains, his last journal and his belongings over more than 1,000 miles to the coast. Seventy-nine followers completed the journey, and his remains went by ship to Britain.
stops.quote: on a journey that took 63 days to the coastal town of Bagamoyo, a distance exceeding 1,000 miles (1,600 km).

notes: Only the dated stages the article gives are dated: the crossing's Linyanti, Luanda dates are given, but the article gives no year for the Falls, Quelimane or the return to Linyanti (the 1853 to 1856 span is not in the article, so years says 1852 to 1873 only). Zambezi expedition: no year is stated beside 10 March or the Shire stage except 1863; Freetown date left year null. Lake Malawi 6 August: article gives no year beside it. Doubtful wp titles: Linyanti (several places), Shupanga, Murchison Cataracts, Chipundu may lack own articles. Zanzibar uses Stone Town (article names it in the memorials list). Left out: Kuruman, Kolobeng, Lake Ngami (before the crossing, and Kuruman is the start of the earlier life), Lake Bangweulu as a separate stop (no date or event beyond sighting), Cahora Bassa rapids, Lake Nyasa explored by others, Mugere (article says the Mugere meeting is a mistake). Article says Livingstone reached Quelimane but gives no 1856 date; his return to Britain in December 1856 is not a stop. Nyangwe massacre: the article notes the diary and the edited journal differ over who started it; the text keeps to the diary entry of 400 killed.
